query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: Rapid, containerless laser melting performed under an inert atmosphere, monitored by high‐speed differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and interpreted via CALPHAD modeling, can accurately and efficiently determine melting temperature, latent heat (enthalpy of fusion), entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and key liquid-phase thermodynamic properties for high‐entropy alloys (HEAs).
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional cast or pre-alloyed HEA ingots with typical microstructural inhomogeneities that can be overcome by containerless processing.
generation.intervention: Apply rapid laser melting in a containerless, inert (argon) environment, while continuously monitoring the sample with high-speed DSC to capture melting/subsolidus transitions, followed by CALPHAD modeling to extract thermodynamic parameters.
generation.conditions: An inert atmosphere (e.g., argon), a containerless processing setup (such as aerodynamic levitation or laser processing to avoid contamination), and high-speed DSC measurement during controlled heating and cooling cycles.
generation.structural_mediator: The induced melt and subsequent rapid solidification minimize interactions with container walls and oxide formation, ensuring that the observed thermal transitions reflect intrinsic material properties.
generation.mechanism: Laser melting rapidly heats small HEA samples in a containerless environment, preventing extrinsic contaminations. The high-speed DSC captures precise thermal events (endothermic peaks corresponding to melting) even under fast heating rates. CALPHAD modeling then uses these signatures, together with established databases (e.g., from Zinkevich’s studies), to quantitatively extract melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, and the volume change associated with the phase change.
generation.predicted_outcome: Measurement of melting-related parameters with quantitative accuracy (e.g., melting temperature within ±5–10°C, latent heat and entropy values within ±5–10% of expected/calculated values, and volume change on the order of 2.5–3.1% contraction) across a compositionally diverse HEA family.
generation.baseline: Previous work using CALPHAD modeling on rare earth systems and containerless processing via laser melting or aerodynamic levitation, as well as high-speed DSC studies on similar complex alloys, indicate that these techniques enable reliable extraction of thermodynamic quantities.
generation.boundary: This approach is expected to be applicable to HEAs that can be melted without significant oxidation or decomposition. It may be less effective for alloys with very high reactivity or those whose thermal signals are obscured by overlapping phase transitions.
generation.uncertainty: While the method is promising based on analogous systems and selected prior evidence, its performance across the full HEA compositional range and at extreme high temperatures (where additional phenomena such as vaporization or complex multi-phase transitions may occur) requires further experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a representative high‐entropy alloy sample and perform rapid, containerless laser melting under a strictly controlled inert atmosphere. Continuously record thermal data using high-speed DSC during multiple heating/cooling cycles. Independently, measure associated volume changes via high-temperature XRD. Use CALPHAD modeling (employing established thermodynamic databases) to predict expected melting temperatures, latent heat, entropy of fusion, and volume change. Compare these predictions to the DSC and XRD measurements.
measurements: DSC melting peak temperature and integrated peak area (for enthalpy of fusion and entropy extraction)
Unit cell parameter refinements from high-temperature XRD to quantify volume changes during melting
Comparison metrics between CALPHAD-simulated and experimental thermodynamic values
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental DSC and XRD measurements differ from the CALPHAD predictions by more than the established error margins (e.g., a discrepancy > ±20°C in melting temperature or > ±15% in latent heat, entropy, or volume change), the approach is considered invalid.

cited_evidence.text: Neutrons, having no electric charge, are a highly penetrating probe for studying the structural and dynamic properties of materials,. Neutron scattering techniques include diffraction, which gives information on the long-range order of crystalline materials, and pair distribution function analysis, which gives information on the local atomic order. Neutron scattering is well-suited for the present work, because the technique is sensitive to the ordering of the multiple TM elements within HEAs, and the experiments may be conducted using special environments for in situ heating and melting. In the present work, neutron scattering studies were performed at the Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Spallation Neutron Source, using the Nanoscale-ordered Materials Diffractometer. The experiments were conducted over a wide temperature range, from room temperature to 1600°C, using an aerodynamic levitator,,. The levitator provides a containerless environment, in which small samples (~2-mm-diameter spheres) are suspended above a conical nozzle with flowing argon gas, and heated with a 250 W CO2 laser operating at a wavelength of 10.6 μm. He critically reviewed all relevant experimental data available before 2006 and evaluated missing fusion enthalpies values based on measured enthalpy of fusion and volume change on melting for Y2O3. In a more recent evaluation by Zhang and Jung [] evaluation, missing data were estimated from liquidus in RE2O3-Al2O3 phase diagrams. However, new measurements for fusion enthalpies [] are in better agreement with Zinkevich’s assessment. Zhang and Jung’s evaluation varies largely with the values proposed by Konings et al. []. Zinkevich [] database for rare earth sesquioxides is openly available at the NIST website [] and was used in this work without any modifications.
